stages.label: Ghurid & Slave Dynasty
stages.detail: Ghurid & Slave (Mamluk) Dynasty: 1192-1290. Muhammad Ghori's 2nd Tarain victory (1192) founds Turkish rule; Qutbuddin Aibak (1206) establishes the Sultanate at Delhi. Iltutmish consolidates; his daughter Raziyya briefly takes the throne; Balban breaks the power of the chahalgani Turkish nobles. Early Mongol pressure on the northwest frontier. Key monuments — Qutb Minar, Arhai-Din-ka-Jhonpra, Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque (Mameluke style).

stages.label: Khalji Dynasty
stages.detail: Khalji Dynasty: 1290-1320. Jalaluddin Khalji ends the Turkish monopoly; Alauddin (1296-1316) imposes market controls in Delhi, abolishes doab iqtas for direct cash taxation, repels Mongol sieges of 1299 and 1303. Malik Kafur's southern campaigns reach Madurai. Seljuk-Khalji architecture — Alai Darwaza, Siri fortress.

stages.label: Tughlaq Dynasty
stages.detail: Tughlaq Dynasty: 1320-1414. Ghiyasuddin founds Tughlaqabad. Muhammad bin Tughlaq's ambitious but failed experiments — Daulatabad transfer (1327), token currency (1330), Khurasan and Qarachil campaigns. Firuz Shah's canals, karkhanas, hereditary iqtas, jizyah as separate tax. Ibn Battuta qazi of Delhi. Barani's Tarikh. Timur sacks Delhi 1398 — effective end of Tughlaq strength.

stages.label: Sayyid & Lodi Dynasties
stages.detail: Sayyid & Lodi Dynasties: 1414-1540. Sayyid rump after Timur; Bahlul Lodi (1451) founds the Afghan Lodi dynasty, annexes Jaunpur (1484). Sikandar Lodi founds Agra (1506), introduces gazz-i-Sikandari, builds octagonal double-domed tombs. Ibrahim Lodi defeated by Babur at Panipat 1526 (era 6 boundary). Sher Shah's interregnum 1540-55 restores Afghan rule briefly.

stages.label: Vijayanagara & Bahmani
stages.detail: Vijayanagara & Bahmani: 1336-1565. Rebellions against Muhammad bin Tughlaq birth the Vijayanagara empire (Harihara-Bukka, 1336) and the Bahmani kingdom (Hasan Gangu, 1347). Four Vijayanagara dynasties — Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu; peak under Krishnadeva Raya (1509-29). Bahmani peaks under Firuz Shah Bahmani and then minister Mahmud Gawan (8 tarafs, Bidar madarasa). Bahmani splits into five Deccan sultanates (1518). Combined Deccan armies crush Vijayanagara at Talikota (1565).

stages.label: Regional Sultanates (N. India)
stages.detail: Regional Sultanates (North India): 1339-1540. Post-Tughlaq fragmentation — Bengal (Ilyas Shahi, Hussain Shahi), Gujarat (Muzaffar Shahi, peak under Mahmud Begarha), Malwa (at Mandu), Jaunpur (Sharqis, 'Shiraz of the East'), Kashmir (Zainul Abidin 'Bud Shah'), Mewar (Rana Kumbha, Rana Sanga). Distinctive provincial architecture schools — Bengal, Pathan (Malwa), Sharqi (Jaunpur), Bijapur (Deccan).

stages.label: Tribes, Nomads & Settled Communities
stages.detail: Tribes, Nomads & Settled Communities. Ahom kingdom in Brahmaputra valley from 1228 (firearms by 1530s); Gond kingdom of Garha Katanga under Rani Durgawati; Rajput clans in western India; Bhils of central/western India; Mundas, Santals of eastern India. Banjaras — trader-nomads supplying grain to Sultanate armies. Shifting cultivation, pastoralism, and gradual sedentarisation.

stages.label: Bhakti & Sufi Movements
stages.detail: Bhakti & Sufi Movements: 1192-1526. Chishti silsila dominant — Muinuddin Chishti → Bakhtiyar Kaki → Baba Farid → Nizamuddin Auliya → Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehli; Suhrawardis accept state patronage; Kashmir Rishi order synthesises Hindu-Muslim elements. Nirguna bhakti (Kabir, Nanak) and saguna (Ramananda, Chaitanya, Vallabhacharya) flourish. Namdev + Maharashtra saints, Shankaradeva in Assam. Common humanist platform emerges across creeds.

stages.label: Culture, Arts & Administration
stages.detail: Culture, Arts & Administration. Amir Khusrau creates the sabaq-i-hindi Persian style, attributed sitar innovation, praises Hindustan. Persian historiography (Barani, Afif, Isami). Sultanate administration — diwan-i-arz/risalat/insha, karkhanas, iqta→jagir evolution, jizyah as separate tax under Firuz, dagh branding, jauhar in Rajput politics. Trabeate yielding to arcuate architecture; social practices (sati, purdah).

stages.label: Mongol / Yuan / Ilkhanate (parallel)
stages.detail: Parallel: Mongol Eurasia. Chagatai Khanate (Trans-Oxiana), Ilkhanate (Iran), Golden Horde (Russia-steppe), Yuan dynasty (China, Kublai Khan). Pax Mongolica stabilises Silk Road; Marco Polo's 1271 journey. Mongol sack of Baghdad (1258) ends the Abbasid caliphate. Black Death travels Mongol trade routes 1346-48, reshaping Eurasian demography.

stages.label: European Renaissance / Reformation
stages.detail: Parallel: European Renaissance & Reformation. Italian city-states (Medici Florence, Venice, Genoa); humanism (Petrarch, Erasmus); Gutenberg press (1440-48) enables print revolution. Art — Leonardo, Michelangelo. Machiavelli's statecraft. Hundred Years' War (1337-1453), Black Death (1347-51), peasant revolts, decline of feudalism. Protestant Reformation (Luther 1517). Age of Exploration — Columbus (1492), Vasco da Gama (1498). Columbian exchange, Atlantic slave trade, plantation economy.

nodes.label: Chishti Silsila
nodes.detail: Most influential Sufi order in medieval India. Full Delhi lineage: Muinuddin Chishti (Ajmer, d.1235) → Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki (Delhi, d.1235) → Baba Farid (Ajodhan/Pakpattan, d.1265) → Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi, d.1325) → Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehli (d.1356) → Bandanawaz Gisudaraz (Gulbarga, d.1422). Emphasised austerity, rejection of state patronage, use of sama (music) for devotion, simple living, and engagement with the lower classes and Hindus. After Chiragh-i-Dehli the order dispersed from Delhi to eastern and southern India.

nodes.label: Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti
nodes.detail: Founder of the Chishti silsila in India (d. 1235). Arrived in India around 1192, shortly after Prithviraj Chauhan's defeat. Settled in Ajmer (already with a sizeable Muslim population) after initial stays in Lahore and Delhi. Did not write books; fame rose with that of his successors. His dargah at Ajmer attracts devotees of all creeds — a pattern repeated across Chishti dargahs. Mughal emperors from Akbar onwards made pilgrimage to the Ajmer dargah.

nodes.label: Sufism
nodes.detail: Muslim mysticism rejecting outward religiosity, emphasising love and devotion to God and compassion to all. Used methods like zikr, contemplation, sama (singing), raqs (dancing). Organised into silsilas under pirs.

nodes.label: Suhrawardi Silsila
nodes.detail: Sufi order active mainly in Punjab, Multan, and Sindh during the Sultanate period. Famous saints: Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan, Shihabuddin Suhrawardi, Hamid-ud-Din Nagori. Unlike Chishtis, Suhrawardis accepted state patronage and held important ecclesiastical posts. Did not believe in extreme poverty or mystic excesses. Entered India at roughly the same time as the Chishtis.

nodes.label: Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki
nodes.detail: Chishti Sufi saint of Delhi (d. 1235), disciple of Muinuddin Chishti. Major preceptor in the Delhi Chishti lineage between Muinuddin and Baba Farid. His dargah in Mehrauli is an important pilgrimage site. Popular debate whether the Qutb Minar is named after him — unlikely, since the tower was originally part of the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque complex and called by that name; the association with Bakhtiyar Kaki is later.

nodes.label: Baba Farid (Farid-ud-Din Ganj-i-Shakar)
nodes.detail: Major Chishti Sufi saint (1173-1265) based at Ajodhan (modern Pakpattan, Pakistani Punjab) and Hansi. Disciple of Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki. Preceptor of Nizamuddin Auliya. Deeply respected in Delhi — crowds thronged on his visits. His verses (in Punjabi) were later included in the Adi Granth of the Sikhs — the only Chishti saint whose words entered Sikh scripture.

nodes.label: Maharashtra Saints
nodes.detail: Maharashtra bhakti saint-poets spanning 13th-17th centuries, centred on Vitthala of Pandharpur (Varkari tradition). Era 5 figures: Jnaneshwar (c.1275-96, Jnaneshwari commentary on Gita in Marathi), Namdev (1270-1350, tailor-poet, travelled to Delhi, verses in Adi Granth), Chokhamela (14th c, Mahar saint), Janabai (14th c, women saint). Later figures — Eknath (1533-99), Tukaram (1608-50), Sakhubai — belong to Mughal era. All focused on Vitthala temple at Pandharpur; rejected ritualism and birth-based social differences.

nodes.label: Namadeva (Namdev)
nodes.detail: Maharashtra bhakti saint (1270-1350). A tailor by trade (some accounts say a bandit before becoming a saint). Composed in Marathi with intense love and devotion to Vitthala of Pandharpur. Travelled widely; is said to have engaged with Sufi saints at Delhi. His verses later included in the Adi Granth of the Sikhs. Pioneer of Marathi bhakti literature alongside Jnaneshwar.

nodes.label: Nathpanthis, Siddhas and Yogis
nodes.detail: Religious groups criticising conventional religion using logical arguments. Advocated renunciation, meditation on formless Ultimate Reality. Used yogasanas, breathing exercises. Many came from artisanal groups including weavers. Questioned authority of the Vedas. Popular among 'low' castes. Gained ground during emergence of new urban centres in the Sultanate period. Influenced Kabir and north Indian nirguna bhakti.

nodes.label: Nasiruddin Chiragh-i-Dehli
nodes.detail: Chishti Sufi saint (d. 1356), successor to Nizamuddin Auliya at Delhi. Called 'Chiragh-i-Dehli' (Lamp of Delhi). After his death the Chishtis no longer had a commanding figure at Delhi — as a result Chishti saints dispersed to eastern and southern India, greatly extending the order's reach.

nodes.label: Rishi Silsilah (Kashmir)
nodes.detail: Indigenous Sufi order of Kashmir combining features of Hinduism and Islam. Founded by Sheikh Noor-ud-din Noorani (Nund Rishi, 1377-1440); spiritually rooted in the earlier Shaiva mystic Lalleshwari (Lal Ded, 14th c). Rishis preached in Kashmiri, mingled with Hindu and Muslim devotees, used yogic practices. Promoted religious synthesis in Kashmir during a period of mass conversion.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Ramananda
nodes.detail: North Indian bhakti saint (late 14th-early 15th c), follower of Ramanuja tradition. Substituted Rama for Vishnu as primary object of devotion. Born Prayag (Allahabad), based at Banaras. Taught bhakti to all four varnas; disregarded ban on inter-caste dining. Disciples drawn from all castes: Ravidas (cobbler), Kabir (weaver), Sena (barber), Sadhana (butcher), Pipa (raja), Dhanna (cultivator). Pioneer of north Indian vernacular bhakti.

nodes.label: Saguna and Nirguna Bhakti
nodes.detail: Two broad categories of bhakti. Saguna (with attributes): worship of specific deities like Shiva, Vishnu, Devi in anthropomorphic forms. Nirguna (without attributes): worship of abstract formless god, rejecting idol worship. Kabir and Guru Nanak were nirguna saints.
nodes.chapter_title: Bhakti-Sufi Traditions - Changes in Religious Beliefs and Devotional Texts

nodes.label: Vallabhacharya
nodes.detail: Tailang Brahman philosopher-saint (1479-1531) who propounded Shuddhadvaita (pure non-dualism). Founded the Pushtimarga path of Krishna devotion centred on Srinathji at Govardhan. Followers (Vallabha sampradaya) emphasise grace (pushti) over personal effort. Influenced the saint-poets including Surdas, one of his ashtachhap disciples.

nodes.label: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu
nodes.detail: Bengal Vaishnava saint (1486-1534). Born in Nadia (a centre of Vedantic rationalism), initiated into Krishna cult at Gaya at age 22. Popularised kirtan (musical congregational worship) as a mystic path — the outside world 'disappeared by dwelling on God's name'. Toured widely including Vrindavan, where he revived the Krishna cult; spent much of later life at Puri. Called God Hari; god-intoxicated ecstatic devotion. Attracted Hindu and some Muslim followers; close ties with Alauddin Hussain Shah's Bengal court. Gaudiya Vaishnavism traces to him.

nodes.label: Dargah Culture
nodes.detail: Tombs/shrines of Sufi saints became pilgrimage centres attracting people of all faiths. Major dargahs: Ajmer (Muinuddin Chishti), Delhi (Nizamuddin Auliya), Fatehpur Sikri (Salim Chishti). Urs (death anniversary) celebrations drew thousands. Kings often sought blessings of Sufi saints.

nodes.label: Guru Nanak
nodes.detail: Founder of Sikhism (1469-1539). Born at Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib) on the Ravi, in a Khatri family. Trained in Persian for his father's accountancy profession but inclined to mysticism. After a mystic vision forsook the world; toured widely — said to have reached Sri Lanka in the south, Mecca and Medina in the west. Composed hymns sung to the rabab played by his lifelong companion Bhai Mardana. Founded centre at Kartarpur with the langar (common kitchen). Taught nam (worship), dan (charity), isnan (purity). Rejected caste, creed, and gender distinctions. Advocated a middle path — spiritual life combined with householder duties. Appointed Lehna (Guru Angad) as successor. No intention of founding a new religion; his teachings birthed Sikhism.

nodes.label: Kabir
nodes.detail: Major nirguna bhakti saint (c.1398-1448, though dating uncertain). Brought up in a Muslim julaha (weaver) family in Banaras. Disciple of Ramananda. Drew from Nath, Sufi, and Vaishnava traditions. Rejected external worship of both Hinduism and Islam — idol-worship, pilgrimages, bathing in holy rivers, namaz, the authority of the Vedas and Quran. Denounced caste, especially untouchability. Emphasised reform of the individual under a true guru; not a social reformer per se. Verses in sakhis (couplets) and pads (songs); compiled in the Bijak by his followers (Kabir Panthis) and included in the Adi Granth of the Sikhs.

nodes.label: Nizamuddin Auliya
nodes.detail: Greatest Chishti Sufi of Delhi (1238-1325). Preceptor Baba Farid. Emphasized love as basis of relationship with God; stressed compassion and generosity. Adopted yogic breathing exercises so thoroughly that yogis called him a sidh ('perfect'). Used local Hindawi dialect with common people. Practised sama (musical recitation) including Hindi verses to maximise impact. Contemporary of seven sultans (Balban to Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq); famously refused to meet Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq — the 'delhi hunuz dur ast' prophecy. Amir Khusrau was his chief devotee and musical companion. His dargah in Delhi remains a major pilgrimage site; adjacent tombs of Khusrau and Jahanara.

nodes.label: Shankaradeva of Assam
nodes.detail: Late 15th century saint from Assam who emphasised devotion to Vishnu. Composed poems and plays in Assamese. Founded namghars (houses of prayer). Teaching called Eka Sarana Nama Dharma (supreme surrender).

nodes.label: Temple Towns
nodes.detail: Pattern of urbanisation where temples were central to economy and society. Rulers endowed temples with land and money. Pilgrims made donations. Temple authorities financed trade and banking.

nodes.label: Panchalas/Vishwakarma Community
nodes.detail: Community of goldsmiths, bronzesmiths, blacksmiths, masons and carpenters essential for temple building. Also built palaces, tanks and reservoirs. Example of craft specialisation in medieval towns.

nodes.label: Sati Practice
nodes.detail: Self-immolation of widows on husband's funeral pyre. Both Al-Biruni and Ibn Battuta recorded this practice. Bernier also described it. Different travellers offered varying perspectives: some described it as voluntary, others as coerced. Became major issue in colonial-era social reform.
nodes.chapter_title: Through the Eyes of Travellers - Perceptions of Society

nodes.label: Amir Khusrau
nodes.detail: Born 1252 at Patiali (Etah, UP); d. 1325, buried in the same compound as his pir Nizamuddin Auliya (whom he survived by less than a day). Served seven Delhi sultans including Balban, Kaiqubad, Jalaluddin, Alauddin Khalji, Qutbuddin Mubarak, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, Muhammad Tughlaq. Called 'tuti-i-hind' (Parrot of India). Took pride in his Indian identity — 'Hindustan is like heaven... Brahmans here are as learned as Aristotle.' Created the sabaq-i-hindi style of Persian poetry. Large Persian output including historical romances. Credited with inventing the sitar (disputed) and introducing Perso-Arabic ragas (aiman, ghora, sanam). Composed the first detailed Persian account of the jauhar at Ranthambhor 1301.

nodes.label: Jagirdari System
nodes.detail: Revenue assignments given to mansabdars as salary. Unlike muqtis, most mansabdars did not reside in or administer jagirs. By Aurangzeb's reign, actual revenue was less than granted sums causing shortages.

nodes.label: Arcuate Architecture
nodes.detail: From the 12th century, arches carried the weight of superstructure above doors and windows. Combined with limestone cement that hardened into concrete, enabling larger and faster construction.

nodes.label: Diwan-i-Arz (Military Department)
nodes.detail: Military department of the Sultanate, headed by the ariz-i-mamalik. Responsible for recruiting, equipping and paying the army (the sultan retained chief command). First established as a separate department under Balban; elaborated by Alauddin Khalji — regular musters, dagh (horse branding), cash salaries (238 tankas/year for a cavalryman).

nodes.label: Diwan-i-Insha
nodes.detail: Sultanate department of state correspondence — formal and confidential communications between the ruler and other sovereigns or subordinate officials. Important office of dabir-i-khas (chief scribe). Persian the standard language.

nodes.label: Diwan-i-Risalat
nodes.detail: Sultanate department dealing with religious matters, pious foundations, stipends for scholars and men of piety. Headed by the chief sadr, usually also the chief qazi. Handled judicial administration; Islamic civil law (sharia) dispensed through qazis across the empire.

nodes.label: Evolution of 'Hindustan'
nodes.detail: 13th century: Minhaj-i-Siraj used it for Punjab, Haryana and Ganga-Yamuna areas under Delhi Sultan. 16th century: Babur used it for geography and culture of the subcontinent. Never originally included south India.

nodes.label: Jizyah
nodes.detail: Poll tax on non-Muslims (zimmis) originating from Arab rule. In Delhi Sultanate initially bundled with land revenue (hard to separate since most cultivators were Hindus). Firuz Tughlaq made it a distinct tax and imposed it on Brahmans (previously exempt). Sikandar Lodi re-imposed after some relaxation. Collected on graduated scale by means; women, children, disabled, indigent exempt. Abolished by Akbar 1564; re-imposed by Aurangzeb 1679.

nodes.label: Royal Karkhanas
nodes.detail: Royal workshops and stores of the Sultanate. Manufactured and stocked costly articles for the king and royal household — silk, gold/silver ware, jewelry, robes of honour. Muhammad Tughlaq's karkhanas produced 2,00,000 robes yearly to gift nobles. Firuz Tughlaq established a separate slave department with 1,80,000 slaves, many employed in karkhanas. A model continued under the Mughals on a grander scale.

nodes.label: Manipravalam
nodes.detail: Literally 'diamonds and corals', referring to a mix of Sanskrit and regional language (Malayalam). The 14th-century text Lilatilakam on grammar and poetics was composed in this style.

nodes.label: Trabeate (Corbelled) Architecture
nodes.detail: Style using horizontal beams across vertical columns for roofs, doors and windows. Used from 7th-13th centuries for temples, mosques, tombs and stepped-wells (baolis).

nodes.label: Amara-Nayaka System
nodes.detail: Major political innovation of Vijayanagara — likely derived from the Delhi Sultanate's iqta system. Military commanders (nayakas, palaiyagars) given territories (amaram) to govern. Collected taxes, retained part for personal use and for maintaining specified foot/horse/elephant forces, and sent fixed tribute/contingent to the king annually. Under Krishnadeva Raya, the central government received only about half the total revenue (12 million pardaos estimate). Nayaks eventually established independent kingdoms (Madurai, Tanjore, Ginjee after Talikota), hastening imperial collapse. Weakened the Chola-era tradition of village self-government.

nodes.label: Harihara and Bukka
nodes.detail: Founders of the Vijayanagara empire in 1336. Legend: feudatories of the Kakatiyas of Warangal, later ministers of the Kampili kingdom in Karnataka. When Muhammad Tughlaq overran Kampili for sheltering a Muslim rebel, they were imprisoned, converted to Islam, and sent back to administer — they then reverted to Hinduism at the guidance of guru Vidyaranya and declared independence. Harihara crowned 1336; Bukka succeeded in 1356 and ruled till 1377. Some modern scholars reject the conversion narrative, seeing them instead as Karnataka nayaks rebelling against Turkish rule. Together they established Vijayanagara as a kind of cooperative brotherly commonwealth.

nodes.label: Sangama Dynasty
nodes.detail: First ruling dynasty of Vijayanagara founded by Harihara and Bukka in 1336. Exercised control until 1485 when supplanted by Saluva military commanders. Built the Hiriya canal drawing water from a dam across the Tungabhadra river.

nodes.label: Vidyaranya
nodes.detail: Hindu sage and guru who (by tradition) re-admitted Harihara and Bukka to Hinduism after their conversion under Muhammad Tughlaq, and blessed the founding of the Vijayanagara empire in 1336. Associated with the Sringeri matha. Historicity of the reconversion narrative is debated.

nodes.label: Bahmani Kingdom
nodes.detail: Deccan sultanate (1347-1518) founded by Hasan Gangu (Alauddin Bahman Shah). Capital Gulbarga, shifted to Bidar under Ahmad Shah I Wali (1424). Rivals of Vijayanagara over Tungabhadra doab, Krishna-Godavari delta, and Konkan. Peak under Firuz Shah Bahmani (1397-1422) and later Mahmud Gawan (minister 1460-81). Split into five successor sultanates — Berar, Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar — after Mahmud Gawan's execution in 1481. Acted as cultural bridge between north and south India.

nodes.label: Deccan Sultanates
nodes.detail: Five successor states of the Bahmani kingdom after Mahmud Gawan's execution 1481 and further fragmentation by 1518: Bijapur (Adil Shahi, Iranian-origin), Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shahi), Golconda (Qutb Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi, earliest to fall — absorbed by Ahmadnagar 1574), Bidar (Barid Shahi). Allied at Talikota 1565 to defeat Vijayanagara. Absorbed one by one into Mughal empire during 17th century — Berar/Ahmadnagar under Akbar-Shah Jahan, Bijapur and Golconda under Aurangzeb 1686-87. Cultural centres — Bijapur's Gol Gumbaz, Golconda's Charminar, Bidar's architecture. Relations with Vijayanagara not always hostile despite religious differences.

nodes.label: Hasan Gangu (Alauddin Bahman Shah)
nodes.detail: Afghan adventurer who founded the Bahmani kingdom in 1347. Rose in service of a Brahman named Gangu (hence Hasan Gangu). As Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah, he traced descent from the mythical Iranian hero Bahman Shah — though Ferishta relates that 'Bahman' was actually a tribute to his Brahman patron. Capital at Gulbarga.

nodes.label: Firuz Shah Bahmani
nodes.detail: Most remarkable Bahmani sultan (1397-1422). Learned in religious sciences, botany, geometry, logic. Spoke Persian, Arabic, Turkish, Telugu, Kannada, Marathi. Built an observatory near Daulatabad. Patronised scholars from Iran and Iraq — wanted to make the Deccan the cultural centre of India. Inducted Hindus on a large scale — Deccani Brahmans rose to prominence in revenue administration. Developed Chaul and Dabhol as ports. Married daughter of Deva Raya I (1420) with legendary splendour. Defeated by Deva Raya I in 1419; abdicated to his brother Ahmad Shah I.

nodes.label: Horse Trade
nodes.detail: Import of horses from Arabia and Central Asia was crucial for warfare. Initially controlled by Arab traders. Local kudirai chettis (horse merchants) also participated. Portuguese arrived 1498 with superior musket technology, becoming important players in regional politics.

nodes.label: Indo-Islamic Architecture at Vijayanagara
nodes.detail: Vijayanagara rulers borrowed and developed Indo-Islamic techniques: arches and domes on gateways, style introduced by Turkish Sultans. Mosque architecture in urban core resembles Hindu mandapas. Shows cultural interaction despite political rivalry with sultanates.

nodes.label: Mahanavami Dibba
nodes.detail: Massive platform in the royal centre, base of 11,000 sq ft rising to 40 ft. Relief carvings on base. Used for Mahanavami/Dasara/Navaratri festival celebrations including worship, animal sacrifice, wrestling, processions. Kings displayed prestige and received tribute from nayakas.

nodes.label: Vijayanagara Fortifications
nodes.detail: Seven concentric lines of forts noted by Abdur Razzaq. Massive masonry without mortar, using wedge-shaped stone blocks. Unique feature: agricultural tracts enclosed within walls to survive sieges. Second line around urban complex, third around royal centre.

nodes.label: Virupaksha Temple
nodes.detail: Temple in the sacred centre of Hampi, dedicated to a form of Shiva. Priests of this temple provided initial information to Colin Mackenzie. One of the longest-surviving structures, with worship continuing to the present day.

nodes.label: Bidar
nodes.detail: Second capital of the Bahmani kingdom from 1424 under Ahmad Shah I Wali, shifted from Gulbarga after the annexation of Warangal. Bidri metalwork (silver/copper inlay on blackened zinc-copper alloy) originated here — named after the city. Mahmud Gawan's madarasa (1472) is a major monument. Became capital of the independent Bidar sultanate after the Bahmani breakup; later absorbed by Bijapur, then the Mughals.

nodes.label: Deva Raya II
nodes.detail: Vijayanagara ruler (1425-46), considered greatest of the Sangama dynasty. Reorganised army to match Bahmani cavalry strength — enlisted 2000 Muslim cavalrymen with jagirs; ordered Hindu soldiers to learn archery from them. Ferishta records 60,000 Hindu archers, 80,000 cavalry, 2,00,000 infantry. Nicolo Conti (1420) and Abdur Razzaq (1440s) visited during his or his father's reign; both praised Vijayanagara's size and wealth. Succession confusion after his death led to the dynasty change (Saluva).

nodes.label: Mahmud Gawan
nodes.detail: Iranian-born trader who rose to become Peshwa (prime minister) and Malik-ut-Tujjar of the Bahmani kingdom for almost 20 years (d. 1481). Militarily overran western coastal areas including Dabhol and Goa. Internal reforms — divided kingdom into 8 tarafs (provinces) with tarafdars; fixed salaries (1 lakh hun/year for 500 horses); set apart khalisa tracts for sultan; attempted land measurement. Built a three-storey madarasa at Bidar (1472) with tiled walls and free food/clothing for 1000 teachers and students. Executed in 1482 at over 70 — victim of Deccani-Afaqi factional strife.

nodes.label: Bijapur (Deccan) Architecture School
nodes.detail: Adil Shahi Bijapur's provincial style (1489-1686) — developed after Bahmani breakup. Features: 3-arched facade, bulbous dome (almost spherical with narrow neck), cornices, iron clamps + strong mortar giving apparently-unsupported ceilings, rich wall carvings. Spans era 5/6 boundary. Major monument — Gol Gumbaz (mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah, completed 1656, 2nd largest dome in the world, famous whispering gallery) — era 6. Ibrahim Rauza (1627) also noteworthy.

nodes.label: Calico
nodes.detail: Term derived from Calicut (Kerala coast) where Portuguese first landed in search of spices. Became the general name for all cotton textiles in European trade.
