nodes.label: Duarte Barbosa
nodes.detail: Portuguese writer who provided detailed account of trade and society in south India after 1500. Part of a wave of European travellers including Jesuit Roberto Nobili and French jeweller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier who documented Indian society.
nodes.chapter_title: Through the Eyes of Travellers - Perceptions of Society

nodes.label: Lotus Mahal
nodes.detail: Beautiful building in the royal centre, named by British travellers. Possibly a council chamber per Mackenzie's map. Combines Hindu and Indo-Islamic architectural elements including arches. Nine towers: one high central tower and eight on sides.

nodes.label: Krishnadeva Raya
nodes.detail: Most famous Vijayanagara ruler (1509-29) of the Tuluva dynasty. Acquired Raichur doab (1512), subdued Orissa (1514), defeated Sultan of Bijapur (1520). Built fine temples and gopurams. Composed Amuktamalyada in Telugu on statecraft. Called 'establisher of the Yavana kingdom'.

nodes.label: Domingo Paes
nodes.detail: Portuguese traveller who visited Vijayanagara in the 16th century during or just after Krishnadeva Raya's reign. Compared the city's size to Rome. Described the royal centre, mahanavami celebrations, water works and gardens in detail.

nodes.label: Rama Raja
nodes.detail: Real power in Vijayanagara under titular ruler Sadashiva Raya (1543-67). Played off the Deccan sultans against each other; concluded a commercial treaty with the Portuguese that stopped horse supply to Bijapur. Defeated Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar in sequence — but this drove them into alliance. The combined army of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda (+ Bidar) inflicted the final defeat at the Battle of Bannihatti (Talikota) in 1565 — Rama Raja was captured and executed on the field.

nodes.label: Battle of Talikota (1565)
nodes.detail: Battle at Rakshasi-Tangadi where combined armies of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda routed Vijayanagara forces led by Rama Raya. City was sacked and totally abandoned. Empire shifted to Penukonda then Chandragiri under Aravidu dynasty. Rama Raya's policy of playing sultans against each other backfired.

nodes.label: Abdur Razzaq Samarqandi
nodes.detail: Persian diplomat who visited south India in the 1440s. Provided one of the most important descriptions of Vijayanagara in the 15th century. Greatly impressed by the fortifications, noting seven lines of forts encircling the city.

nodes.label: Bidri Work
nodes.detail: Inlay work in copper and silver so famous from Bidar that it was named after the city. Represents the high-quality metalwork craftsmanship of medieval Indian towns.

nodes.label: Colin Mackenzie
nodes.detail: Engineer, surveyor and cartographer who discovered Hampi ruins in 1800. First Surveyor General of India (1815-1821). Prepared first survey map of Vijayanagara based on memories of Virupaksha temple priests and Pampadevi shrine. Collected local histories for colonial governance.

nodes.label: Hampi (Vijayanagara)
nodes.detail: Capital of Vijayanagara Empire founded 1336 in natural basin of Tungabhadra river surrounded by granite hills. Three zones: sacred centre (Virupaksha + Vitthala temples), urban core (markets, mosques, merchant quarters), royal centre (Mahanavami Dibba, Lotus Mahal). Seven lines of fortifications, enclosing even agricultural tracts to survive sieges. Water drawn from Kamalapuram tank and Hiriya canal. Bustled with merchants, festivals (Mahanavami/Dasara). Sacked in 1565 after Battle of Talikota; abandoned. Rediscovered by Colin Mackenzie in 1800.

nodes.label: Vijayanagara Empire
nodes.detail: Founded 1336 by Harihara and Bukka at the guidance of guru Vidyaranya. City Hampi named after mother-goddess Pampadevi. Four dynasties — Sangama (1336-1485), Saluva (1485-1505), Tuluva (1505-1570, Krishnadeva Raya), Aravidu (1570-1646). Also called Karnataka Samrajyamu in contemporary Telugu sources. Reached extreme south of peninsula; major rival of Bahmani over Tungabhadra doab/Krishna-Godavari delta/Konkan. Sacked 1565 after Battle of Rakshasi-Tangadi (Talikota/Bannihatti). Empire shifted to Penukonda and Chandragiri under Aravidu dynasty but never recovered.

nodes.label: Prithviraja III (Prithviraj Chauhan)
nodes.detail: Best-known Chahamana ruler (1168-1192) who controlled Delhi and Ajmer. Defeated Afghan ruler Muhammad Ghori in 1191 at the First Battle of Tarain but lost to him in 1192 at the Second Battle.

nodes.label: Muizzuddin Muhammad (Muhammad of Ghur)
nodes.detail: Ghurid ruler (1173-1206) who established Turkish rule in north India. Conquered Multan and Uchch (1175), defeated by Gujarat ruler near Mount Abu (1178), captured Peshawar/Lahore/Sialkot by 1190. Defeated at 1st Tarain (1191) by Prithviraj III; decisive victor at 2nd Tarain (1192). Chandawar (1194) against Jaichandra of Kanauj extended Turkish rule to Ganga valley. Assassinated 1206 by a Muslim fanatic while suppressing the Khokhar rebellion. Political achievements in India greater than Mahmud Ghazni despite Mahmud's larger empire outside India.

nodes.label: Quwwat al-Islam Mosque
nodes.detail: Congregational mosque of the first city built by the Delhi Sultans. Built in the 1190s, enlarged by Iltutmish and Alauddin Khalji. Associated with the Qutb Minar. Earliest example of Sultanate architecture.

nodes.label: Arhai Din Ka Jhonpra (Ajmer)
nodes.detail: Mosque at Ajmer, converted by Qutbuddin Aibak around 1199 from an older Sanskrit college/Jain temple (reusing Hindu/Jain pillars — many carvings still visible). Elaborately carved 7-arch screen of Quranic verses intertwined with floral motifs added in front of the earlier sanctum. Alongside Delhi's Quwwat-ul-Islam, among the earliest Sultanate mosques — defining monument of the Mameluke style. Popular name 'Two and a Half Day Shed' per folk etymology.

nodes.label: Qutb Minar
nodes.detail: Tapering tower (originally 71.4 m high, 5 storeys) — ground storey by Qutbuddin Aibak, storeys 2-4 by Iltutmish, top (5th) storey added by Firuz Shah Tughlaq after lightning damage. Sikander Lodi repaired further earthquake damage. Part of the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque complex, not originally named for Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki. Effect derived from projected-yet-linked balconies, alternating red and white sandstone with marble panels, and ribbed vertical fluting. Alai Darwaza (1311) added by Alauddin Khalji as entrance. Alauddin planned a minar twice its height but died before it was begun.

nodes.label: Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji
nodes.detail: Khalji officer under Muhammad Ghori who conquered Bihar and Bengal (1204). Destroyed Buddhist monasteries of Nalanda and Vikramasila in Bihar raids. Attacked Sena capital Nadia disguised as horse-merchant; Sena ruler Lakshmana Sena fled to Sonargaon. Made Lakhnauti the new Muslim capital of Bengal. Died after disastrous Assam expedition against Magh rulers — stabbed by his own amir while sick and defeated.

nodes.label: Delhi Sultanate
nodes.detail: Five dynasties ruling from Delhi (1206-1526): Early Turkish, Khalji, Tughluq, Sayyid and Lodi. Transformed Delhi from a commercial centre to capital controlling vast areas. Administration used Persian.

nodes.label: Mameluke Style (Slave Dynasty Architecture)
nodes.detail: Indo-Islamic architectural style of the Slave/Ilbari dynasty (1206-1290). Mostly remodellings of existing Hindu structures. Qutb Minar begun by Aibak (ground floor), next three storeys by Iltutmish. Key examples: Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, Arhai-Din-ka-Jhonpra (Ajmer, converted from a Jain college). Decoration uses arabesque + intertwined Quranic script — no human/animal figures.

nodes.label: Qutbuddin Aibak
nodes.detail: Turkish slave of Muhammad Ghori; first Sultan of Delhi (1206-10), ruling from Lahore. Severed Sultanate's links with Ghazni, enabling an India-based state. Began construction of Qutb Minar. Defeated Bhima III of Gujarat; conquered forts at Bayana, Gwaliyar, Kalinjar, Mahoba, Khajuraho. Died 1210 from injuries in a fall from horseback while playing chaugan (polo). Succeeded by his son-in-law Iltutmish.

nodes.label: Shamsuddin Iltutmish
nodes.detail: Sultan who ruled 1210-1236, consolidated the Delhi Sultanate. Favoured specially trained slaves (bandagan) for political offices. His daughter Raziyya became Sultan in 1236. Built parts of Qutb Minar.

nodes.label: Mongol Invasions of India
nodes.detail: Multiple Mongol incursions into the Indian subcontinent from the 13th to 14th centuries. Genghis Khan reached the Indus during Jalal-ud-din Khilji's reign (c. 1221). Later invasions were repelled by Alauddin Khilji. The Delhi Sultanate's military preparedness was significantly shaped by the Mongol threat.

nodes.label: Raziyya Sultan
nodes.detail: Iltutmish's daughter who became Sultan in 1236, more able than her brothers. Chronicler Minhaj-i Siraj acknowledged her ability but was uncomfortable with a woman ruler. Removed from throne in 1240.

nodes.label: Bandagan (Slave Officers)
nodes.detail: Specially purchased slaves trained for military service and important political offices. Favoured by Iltutmish because they were totally dependent on the Sultan. Loyal to master but not to heirs.

nodes.label: Ghiyasuddin Balban
nodes.detail: Sultan 1266-1287 who consolidated the Delhi Sultanate. A Sanskrit prashasti claimed his empire stretched from Bengal to Ghazni including south India, though historians regard these as exaggerated.

nodes.label: Chahalgani (Group of Forty)
nodes.detail: Group of forty privileged Turkish nobles/slaves who dominated early Delhi Sultanate politics after Iltutmish. Acted as kingmakers on his death, initially opposing Raziya. Balban (1266-87) systematically broke their power — first by excluding non-Turks to appease them, then by raising monarchy above all nobles, ultimately eliminating the group's kingmaking role.

nodes.label: Jalaluddin Khalji
nodes.detail: Founder of the Khalji dynasty (1290-96), first non-Turk sultan. Warden of the marches in the northwest who had fought Mongols. Mild ruler — held that state should rest on the willing support of the governed, and that an Islamic state was impossible with a Hindu majority. Defeated Mongols under Abdullah (Halaku's grandson) near Tabarhinda 1292. Treacherously murdered by his nephew and son-in-law Alauddin Khalji at Kara 1296.

nodes.label: Alauddin Khalji
nodes.detail: Sultan 1296-1316 who expanded into south India, raised a large standing army in Siri to counter Mongols, controlled market prices in Delhi, fixed taxes at 50% of produce, and cancelled chieftains' tax rights.

nodes.label: Iqta System
nodes.detail: Land-revenue assignment system brought from West Asia by the Turks. A Turkish chief was allotted a tract as iqta from which he collected revenue; in return he maintained troops for the sultan. Not hereditary — at the sultan's pleasure, transferable. The sultan drew revenue directly from khalisa lands. Evolved: initially muqtis kept almost all revenue (early Sultanate); Balban began tighter control; Alauddin abolished doab iqtas (cash salaries instead); Muhammad Tughlaq restored and expanded; Firuz Tughlaq made iqtas hereditary — weakening the system and undermining central control. Became the basis of the Mughal jagirdari system.

nodes.label: Kharaj (Land Tax)
nodes.detail: Tax on cultivation amounting to about 50% of the peasant's produce under Alauddin Khalji. One of three main taxes along with taxes on cattle and houses. Central to Sultanate revenue.

nodes.label: Seljuk Style (Khalji Architecture)
nodes.detail: Architectural style of the Khalji dynasty (1290-1320), named for its Seljuk Turkish influences. Prominence of the arcuate (arch) method over the trabeate (lintel-beam). First widespread use of mortar as cementing agent. Red sandstone dominant. True dome first constructed on scientific principles at the Alai Darwaza. Alauddin built the fortress-city of Siri — his second capital — as part of the Mongol-defense infrastructure.

nodes.label: Mongol Invasions of Delhi Sultanate
nodes.detail: Sustained Mongol threat to north India from 1221 (Changez Khan pursuing Jalaluddin to Indus) through 1327 (Tarmashrin under Muhammad Tughlaq). Early attacks by Chagatai Mongols of Trans-Oxiana. Key invasions: 1292 — Abdullah (Halaku's grandson) defeated by Jalaluddin Khalji near Tabarhinda (4000 Mongol converts settled near Delhi). 1297-1303 — Dawa Khan's sustained campaigns; 1299 Qutlugh Khwaja's 2,00,000 entered Delhi streets; 1303 Mongols camped outside Siri two months during Alauddin's Chittor campaign. Prompted Alauddin's army reforms (market controls, dagh, 300,000 cavalry, construction of Siri). Mongol threat eased with Dawa Khan's death 1306 and civil war among Chagatais. 1327 Tarmashrin reached Meerut but was defeated by Muhammad Tughlaq near Jhelum.

nodes.label: Alauddin's Market Controls
nodes.detail: Alauddin Khalji's market regulations (c.1300) — three dedicated markets at Delhi (foodgrains; costly cloth; horses/slaves/cattle), each under a high officer (shahna) who maintained merchant registers and strictly controlled prices. Designed primarily to enable a large standing army against Mongols by keeping salaries low — cavalryman paid 238 tankas/year. Mechanics: doab land revenue raised to 50% of produce and collected directly (no iqta), forcing peasants to sell cheap to registered banjaras who brought grain to Delhi at fixed prices. State warehouses stocked against famine. Very harsh enforcement — false weights punished, no variation allowed even during famine. Barani: 'wheat 7½ jitals per man, the permanence of prices was a wonder of the age.' Collapsed with Alauddin's death.

nodes.label: Siri (Alauddin's capital)
nodes.detail: Second city of Delhi, built by Alauddin Khalji as a base to counter Mongol invasions (from 1303 onwards). Strongly fortified; housed his standing army. Alauddin camped at Siri during the 1303 Mongol siege by Qutlugh Khwaja. Hazar Sutun (Palace of a Thousand Pillars) was here — described in detail by Ibn Battuta. Mostly ruined; remnants near modern Hauz Khas and Shahpur Jat.

nodes.label: Malik Kafur
nodes.detail: Alauddin Khalji's slave general; captured at Cambay during the 1299 Gujarat campaign. Led two south Indian expeditions (1309-11): against Warangal (Kakatiyas/Telangana) and then Dwara Samudra (Hoysalas/Karnataka) and Mabar (Pandyas/Tamil Nadu), reaching Madurai — first Muslim forces that far south. Plundered Chidambaram temple. Made malik-naib (vice-regent). After Alauddin's death 1316 raised a minor son to throne, imprisoned/blinded the others; killed by palace guards.

nodes.label: Alai Darwaza
nodes.detail: Entrance gateway to the Qutb complex, built by Alauddin Khalji in 1311. Defining monument of the Seljuk/Khalji style — red sandstone with white marble inlay. Prominent use of the arcuate (arch) method; first building in India with a true dome constructed on correct scientific principles. Pleasing arch proportions; lotus-bud fringes on arch undersides. Alauddin had planned a minaret twice the height of Qutb Minar but died before work could begin.

nodes.label: Dagh (Horse-branding) System
nodes.detail: Mandatory branding of cavalry horses introduced by Alauddin Khalji to prevent soldiers from bringing poor-quality horses to muster. Combined with descriptive rolls (chehra) of each soldier. Part of Alauddin's army reforms that enabled his Mongol resistance and south Indian conquests. Revived and formalised by Sher Shah and Akbar (as part of the Mansabdari system).

nodes.label: Jauhar Ceremony
nodes.detail: Rajput ritual of collective self-immolation by women (and suicidal last charge by warriors, called saka) when fort defeat was imminent. First Persian description: Ranthambhor 1301 (fall to Alauddin Khalji) by Amir Khusrau. Famous instances — Chittor 1303 (Padmini legend, Ratan Singh's queens), Chittor 1535 (Rani Karnavati), Champaner 1484, Chittor 1568 (under Akbar). Ranthambhor jauhar also saw the Mongol refugees die fighting alongside Hamirdeva.

nodes.label: Temple Destruction in Medieval India
nodes.detail: Not unique to Muslim rulers. Pandyan king looted Buddhist temples in Lanka. Chola Rajendra I seized statues from defeated rulers. Mahmud targeted Somnath. Part of political culture of demonstrating military success.

nodes.label: Sumptuary Laws in France
nodes.detail: From 1294 to 1789 French society had strict dress codes regulating what each social class could wear. Only royalty could wear ermine, silk, velvet and brocade. French Revolution ended these distinctions.

nodes.label: Petrarch
nodes.detail: Italian scholar and poet (1304-1374) often called the 'Father of Humanism'. Rediscovered and promoted classical Latin texts by Cicero and others. His sonnets to Laura established a poetic tradition. Coined the idea of the 'Dark Ages' for the medieval period, looking back to classical antiquity as a golden age.

nodes.label: Hundred Years' War
nodes.detail: Series of conflicts between England and France (1337-1453) over territorial and dynastic claims. Saw the rise of infantry and longbow over mounted knights, undermining feudal warfare. Joan of Arc's role rallied French national sentiment. Ended with French victory and contributed to the decline of feudalism and rise of nation-states.

nodes.label: Black Death in Europe
nodes.detail: Bubonic plague pandemic that devastated Europe between 1347-1353, killing an estimated one-third of the population (25 million). Arrived via trade routes from Central Asia. Led to acute labour shortage which empowered surviving peasants, raised wages, and weakened serfdom. Triggered social upheaval and religious crisis.

nodes.label: Decline of Feudalism
nodes.detail: Feudalism declined from the 14th century due to multiple factors: the Black Death empowered peasants through labour scarcity, the rise of towns and commerce created a money economy, centralising monarchs curbed noble power, gunpowder made castles and mounted knights obsolete, and the Crusades drained feudal resources.

nodes.label: Italian City-States
nodes.detail: Wealthy, independent urban centres like Florence, Venice, Genoa, and Milan that were the cradles of the Renaissance. Prospered from Mediterranean trade, banking, and textile production. Governed as republics or by ruling families (like the Medici in Florence). Their wealth enabled patronage of art, architecture, and learning.

nodes.label: Renaissance
nodes.detail: Cultural and intellectual movement that began in Italy in the 14th century and spread across Europe through the 16th century. Meaning 'rebirth', it revived interest in classical Greek and Roman art, philosophy, and literature. Marked the transition from medieval to modern worldview with emphasis on humanism, individualism, and secularism.

nodes.label: Peasant Revolts
nodes.detail: Uprisings by peasants against feudal lords and heavy taxation, particularly after the Black Death. The English Peasants' Revolt (1381) and the French Jacquerie (1358) were major examples. Triggered by attempts to reimpose pre-plague labour obligations. Though suppressed, they signalled the weakening of feudalism.

nodes.label: Revival of Classical Antiquity
nodes.detail: Rediscovery and study of Greek and Roman texts, art, and philosophy that drove the Renaissance. Facilitated by the fall of Constantinople (1453) which sent Greek scholars and manuscripts westward. Scholars studied classical Latin and Greek, translating works of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and others. Universities became centres of classical learning.

nodes.label: Age of Exploration
nodes.detail: Period from the 15th-17th centuries when European nations explored and colonised distant lands. Driven by trade, religion, and curiosity. Portugal (under Henry the Navigator) led early exploration of Africa. Columbus reached the Americas (1492). Vasco da Gama reached India (1498). Magellan's expedition circumnavigated the globe (1522).

nodes.label: Humanism
nodes.detail: Intellectual movement at the core of the Renaissance emphasising the study of classical texts (studia humanitatis), human potential, and rational inquiry. Humanists like Petrarch, Erasmus, and Thomas More promoted education, critical thinking, and civic virtue. Shifted focus from purely theological concerns to human experience and achievement.

nodes.label: Printing Press (Gutenberg)
nodes.detail: Johannes Gutenberg invented the movable type printing press in Mainz, Germany around 1440. Revolutionised the spread of knowledge by making books cheaper and more widely available. The Gutenberg Bible (1455) was among the first major works printed. Enabled the rapid spread of Renaissance ideas and later the Reformation.

nodes.label: Print Revolution
nodes.detail: Shift from hand-copied manuscripts to mechanical printing transformed knowledge access. Books became cheaper and available to wider population. Created new reading culture and spread of ideas across Europe.
nodes.chapter_title: Print Culture and the Modern World

nodes.label: Leonardo da Vinci
nodes.detail: Italian polymath (1452-1519) often regarded as the ideal 'Renaissance man'. Painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. Also an engineer, anatomist, inventor, and scientist. His notebooks contain designs for flying machines, tanks, and anatomical studies. Epitomised the Renaissance spirit of curiosity and versatility.

nodes.label: Medici Family
nodes.detail: Powerful banking family that effectively ruled Florence for much of the 15th-16th centuries. Lorenzo de' Medici ('the Magnificent', r. 1469-1492) was the most famous patron. The family supported artists like Michelangelo and Botticelli, funded libraries, and shaped Renaissance culture. Produced four popes.

nodes.label: Renaissance Art
nodes.detail: Art underwent transformation with techniques like perspective, chiaroscuro (light and shadow), and anatomical accuracy. Shifted from religious iconography to include secular subjects, portraits, and classical mythology. Artists gained individual fame (unlike anonymous medieval craftsmen). Major figures: Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael, Botticelli.

nodes.label: Erasmus of Rotterdam
nodes.detail: Dutch humanist scholar (1466-1536), the most influential intellectual of the Northern Renaissance. His 'In Praise of Folly' satirised Church corruption and superstition. Produced a critical edition of the Greek New Testament. Advocated reform within the Church rather than separation. Influenced both Catholics and Protestants.

nodes.label: Niccolo Machiavelli
nodes.detail: Italian political philosopher (1469-1527) from Florence. His work 'The Prince' (1513) analysed political power with cold pragmatism, separating politics from morality. Argued that rulers should use any means to maintain power and stability. Considered the founder of modern political science.

nodes.label: Michelangelo
nodes.detail: Italian sculptor, painter, and architect (1475-1564). Created the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel and the sculpture of David. Designed the dome of St. Peter's Basilica. His work combined classical forms with emotional intensity. Considered one of the greatest artists of all time.

nodes.label: Columbian Exchange
nodes.detail: Post-1492 exchange of plants, animals, diseases between Americas and rest of world. Potatoes and corn transformed European diets. Smallpox decimated American populations. Silver from Americas financed European trade with Asia.
nodes.chapter_title: The Making of a Global World

nodes.label: European Colonisation of the Americas
nodes.detail: Beginning with Columbus's arrival in 1492, Spanish, Portuguese, English, French, and Dutch colonised the Americas. The Spanish conquered the Aztec and Inca empires. English colonies on the east coast eventually became the United States. Colonisation brought devastation through disease, enslavement, and cultural destruction of indigenous peoples.

nodes.label: Plantation Economy
nodes.detail: Large-scale agricultural estates in the Americas producing cash crops (sugar, tobacco, cotton, coffee) for European markets. Relied heavily on enslaved African labour after indigenous populations declined. The plantation system enriched colonial powers, fuelled the Atlantic slave trade, and shaped the racial and economic structures of the Americas.

nodes.label: Atlantic Slave Trade
nodes.detail: Forced transportation of an estimated 12-15 million Africans to the Americas between the 16th and 19th centuries. Part of the triangular trade connecting Europe, Africa, and the Americas. Europeans traded manufactured goods for African captives, who were sold into plantation slavery. One of the largest forced migrations in human history.

nodes.label: Martin Luther
nodes.detail: German monk and theologian (1483-1546) who initiated the Protestant Reformation by posting his 95 Theses in Wittenberg in 1517. Argued that salvation comes through faith alone (sola fide) and scripture alone (sola scriptura), not through Church rituals or papal authority. Translated the Bible into German, making it accessible to common people.

nodes.label: Protestant Reformation
nodes.detail: Religious movement begun by Martin Luther in 1517 that challenged Catholic Church doctrines and papal authority. Luther's 95 Theses criticised indulgences and corruption. Led to the establishment of Protestant churches (Lutheran, Calvinist, Anglican). Split Western Christianity and triggered religious wars across Europe.

nodes.label: Rise of Vernacular Literature
nodes.detail: Shift from Latin to local languages in literature and official communication. Dante's 'Divine Comedy' in Italian, Chaucer's 'Canterbury Tales' in English, and Luther's German Bible were landmarks. The printing press accelerated this shift. Vernacular languages became vehicles for national identity and wider literacy.

nodes.label: Chagatai Khanate
nodes.detail: One of the four successor states of the Mongol Empire, named after Genghis Khan's second son Chagatai. Covered Central Asia including modern Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and parts of Afghanistan. Gradually converted to Islam. Eventually fragmented, with Timur emerging from its western portion.

nodes.label: Golden Horde
nodes.detail: The western Mongol khanate founded by Batu Khan (Genghis Khan's grandson) covering Russia, Ukraine, and parts of Central Asia. Ruled from Sarai on the Volga River. Imposed tribute on Russian principalities for over two centuries. Converted to Islam in the early 14th century. Declined by the 15th century.

nodes.label: Pax Mongolica
nodes.detail: Period of relative peace and stability across Eurasia under Mongol rule (c. 1250-1350). Enabled safe long-distance trade along the Silk Road. Facilitated exchange of goods, technologies, ideas, and diseases between China, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. Also transmitted the Black Death.

nodes.label: Ilkhanate
nodes.detail: Mongol khanate established by Hulagu Khan (Genghis Khan's grandson) in Persia and the Middle East after the sack of Baghdad (1258). Ended the Abbasid Caliphate. Rulers eventually converted to Islam. Fell in 1335. Facilitated cultural and scientific exchange between China, Persia, and Europe.

nodes.label: Sack of Baghdad (1258)
nodes.detail: Hulagu Khan's Mongol forces besieged and destroyed Baghdad in 1258, killing the last Abbasid Caliph al-Musta'sim. The destruction of the House of Wisdom and its libraries was a catastrophic loss for Islamic civilisation. Ended the Abbasid Caliphate and shifted the centre of Islamic power.

nodes.label: Kublai Khan
nodes.detail: Grandson of Genghis Khan (r. 1260-1294), he completed the conquest of China and founded the Yuan Dynasty (1271-1368). Moved the capital to Khanbaliq (Beijing). Attempted invasions of Japan and Southeast Asia. Hosted Marco Polo. Under him the Mongol Empire effectively split into four khanates.

nodes.label: Silk Road under Mongols
nodes.detail: The Mongol Empire revitalised the Silk Road by providing security and infrastructure across Eurasia. Established a postal relay system (yam) with rest stations. Merchants, missionaries, and diplomats travelled freely. Marco Polo's journey to Kublai Khan's court exemplifies this connectivity.

nodes.label: Marco Polo
nodes.detail: Venetian merchant and explorer (1254-1324) who travelled to Kublai Khan's China and spent about 17 years in the Mongol Empire. His account, 'The Travels of Marco Polo', introduced Europeans to the wealth and sophistication of Asia. While some details are disputed, it stimulated European interest in the East.

nodes.label: Yuan Dynasty
nodes.detail: Mongol dynasty established by Kublai Khan in China (1271-1368). First foreign dynasty to rule all of China. Maintained Mongol identity while adopting Chinese administrative practices. Promoted trade along the Silk Road. Overthrown by the Ming Dynasty after peasant revolts.

nodes.label: Black Death and Mongol Trade Routes
nodes.detail: The bubonic plague (Black Death) spread along Mongol trade routes from Central Asia to Europe in the 1340s, killing an estimated one-third of Europe's population. The same connectivity that facilitated trade and cultural exchange also transmitted disease. This was an unintended consequence of the Pax Mongolica.

nodes.label: Mewar Kingdom
nodes.detail: Rajput kingdom in southern Rajasthan. Virtual founder Bapa Rawal (Guhilot clan, 7th c). Chittor as capital. After Alauddin Khalji ousted Ratan Singh in 1303, the Sishodia branch (formerly Guhilot feudatories) took over. Rose to prominence under Rana Kumbha (1433-68) and Rana Sanga (1508-28). Survived as independent Rajput state through Sultanate and Mughal periods; eventually Mughal vassal after Akbar's Chittor siege 1568.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Kashmir Sultanate
nodes.detail: Muslim rule established in Kashmir c.1339 after Mongol leader Dalucha's devastating 1320 raid discredited the Hindu government. Baramulla route facilitated incursion of Muslim saints and Central Asian refugees. Sikandar Butshikan (1389-1413) persecuted Brahmans; Zainul Abidin 'Bud Shah' (1420-70) reversed policy and fostered cultural synthesis. Rishi silsilah combined Hindu and Muslim features. Annexed by Mughals under Akbar 1586.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Bengal Architecture School
nodes.detail: Bengal Sultanate's provincial architectural style (14th-16th c). Characterised by use of bricks and black marble. Adopted 'Bangla roof' — sloping/curved roof resembling a thatched bamboo hut, originally a Pala-Sena temple feature, later carried into Mughal architecture as the bangla dome. Key monuments: Adina Mosque (Pandua, c.1375 — largest mosque in Indian subcontinent at its time), Qadam Rasul mosque (Gaur), Eklakhi Mausoleum (Pandua), Sixty Dome Mosque (Bagerhat).

nodes.label: Bengal Sultanate
nodes.detail: Independent from Delhi from 1338 onwards; Ilyas Shahi dynasty founded 1342 by Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah. Capital Pandua, later Gaur. Distinct architectural style using stone and brick. Firuz Tughlaq failed twice to subdue Ilyas and his son Sikandar (who retreated to Ekdala fort). After 200 years of independence, Sher Shah conquered Bengal 1538. Major patron of Bengali literature. Brief Hindu interregnum under Raja Ganesh early 15th c.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Adina Mosque (Pandua)
nodes.detail: Largest mosque of the Indian subcontinent at its time, built 1373-75 by Sultan Sikandar Shah of Bengal at Pandua. Reused stones from destroyed Hindu temples. Long rectangular plan with huge central courtyard; 260 pillars; uniquely large mihrab ornamented with mouldings. A signature Bengal School example — Islamic form with local brick-and-stone material.

nodes.label: Sikandar Shah Butshikan
nodes.detail: Kashmir sultan (1389-1413) known as 'butshikan' (idol-breaker). Ordered all Brahmans to convert to Islam or leave Kashmir; temples destroyed; gold/silver idols melted for currency. Policy implemented by his Hindu-convert minister Suha Bhatt. Led to mass exodus of Brahmans and Hindu learning from the valley. Reversed under his grandson Zainul Abidin.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Jaunpur (Sharqi) Architecture School
nodes.detail: Sharqi provincial style at Jaunpur (1394-1484). Distinctive: bold forceful characters painted on huge screens at centre/side bays of prayer halls; no minars (like Pathan). Unlike Delhi style — emphasis on monumental propylons/facades with soaring arches. Key monuments: Atala Mosque (1408, earliest/most influential), Jami Masjid Jaunpur, Lal Darwaza Mosque.

nodes.label: Jaunpur Sultanate (Sharqis)
nodes.detail: Independent sultanate (1394-1484) in eastern UP founded by Malik Sarwar — formerly wazir of Firuz Tughlaq, titled Malik-us-Sharq (Lord of the East), whence 'Sharqi'. Capital Jaunpur — 'Shiraz of the East'. Distinct architectural style with lofty gates and huge arches. Great patrons of learning. Malik Muhammad Jaisi composed Padmavat here. Great musical patronage under Husain Shah Sharqi. Annexed by Bahlul Lodi 1484 after long Delhi-Jaunpur rivalry for the Ganga-Yamuna valley.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Malwa Sultanate
nodes.detail: Independent from 1401 after Timur's invasion; high plateau between Narmada and Tapti controlling trunk routes Gujarat↔North and North↔South. Capital shifted from Dhar to Mandu. Rival of Gujarat and Mewar in the cockpit struggle for north India. Peak under Mahmud Khalji (1436-69). Internal factionalism allowed Rana Sanga of Mewar to defeat Mahmud II at Khatoli 1517 and annex eastern Malwa. Finally absorbed by Mughals under Akbar 1562.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Malwa (Pathan) Architecture School
nodes.detail: Malwa Sultanate's provincial style centred at Mandu. Also known as 'Pathan School'. Features: coloured stones/marbles; large windows (some European influence); ornate arches and pillars; stairs used aesthetically; NO minars. Environmental adaptation — baulis in premises, lightly-arched airy pavilions, locally available materials, Tughlaq batter. Key monuments: Hindola Mahal, Jahaz Mahal, Rani Roopmati Pavilion, Ashrafi Mahal, Jami Masjid Mandu.

nodes.label: Mandu
nodes.detail: Second capital of Malwa Sultanate, shifted from Dhar. Highly defensible plateau location with natural beauty. Distinctive massive architecture on lofty plinths, using coloured/glazed tiles. Landmark buildings: Jama Masjid, Hindola Mahal, Jahaz Mahal, Hushang Shah's tomb (first marble tomb in India), Rewa Kund and Rupmati Pavilion.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Hushang Shah
nodes.detail: Early Malwa sultan (1406-35) known for religious toleration. Allowed Rajput migration to Malwa (brothers of Rana Mokal of Mewar granted jagirs). Lalitpur temple inscription shows no restrictions on temple construction under him. Patronised Jain merchants; Nardeva Soni was his treasurer. His tomb at Mandu is among the earliest marble tombs in India — said to have been studied by Shah Jahan's architects before the Taj Mahal.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Gujarat Sultanate
nodes.detail: Independent sultanate from 1407 under Zafar Khan (Muzaffar Shah), whose father Sadharan was a Rajput convert whose sister had married Firuz Tughlaq. Initial capital at Patan, shifted to Ahmedabad (founded 1411). Peak under Mahmud Begarha (1459-1511). Annexed Girnar, Champaner; sacked Dwarka. Dealt with Portuguese naval threat through alliance with Ottomans. Rich ports (Cambay, Surat) and textile industry. Absorbed by Akbar 1572-73.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Atala Mosque (Jaunpur)
nodes.detail: Earliest major Sharqi monument, built 1408 by Ibrahim Shah Sharqi at Jaunpur. Signature Sharqi style — towering central propylon with huge recessed arch dominating the facade; bold geometric patterns on screen. Built on the site of an earlier Hindu temple (reused materials). Model for later Sharqi monuments.

nodes.label: Ahmad Shah I of Gujarat
nodes.detail: Gujarat sultan (1411-43), real founder of the kingdom. Shifted capital from Patan to the new city of Ahmedabad (foundation laid 1413). Developed a distinct Gujarat architectural style — slender turrets, exquisite stone-carving, highly ornate brackets — drawing on Jain temple architecture. Built Jama Masjid and Tin Darwaza at Ahmedabad. Imposed jizyah on Hindus (not levied earlier); levelled temples at Sidhpur. But inducted Hindu merchants Manik Chand and Motichand as ministers; had his own son-in-law executed for murder.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Ahmedabad
nodes.detail: Capital of Gujarat Sultanate, founded 1411 by Ahmad Shah I (laid 1413). Distinct architectural style blending Gujarat Jain tradition with Sultanate forms. Landmark buildings: Jama Masjid, Tin Darwaza, later Sidi Saiyyed Mosque. Major centre of textile production — zari (gold lace) work. Renamed Karnavati briefly. Later a Mughal province capital.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Zainul Abidin (Bud Shah)
nodes.detail: Greatest Muslim monarch of Kashmir (1420-70), called 'Bud Shah' (Great Sultan). Reversed Sikandar Butshikan's anti-Hindu policies: cancelled Brahman persecution, restored temples and land grants, abolished jizyah and cow slaughter, even withdrew the ban on sati (in deference to Hindu wishes). Hindus held high office (Sriya Bhatt was chief justice). Sent envoys to Samarqand to learn paper-making and book-binding; fostered shawl-making, stone-cutting, musket-making, fireworks. Had Rajatarangini and Mahabharata translated to Persian. Built Zaina Lanka, an artificial island in Wular Lake. Unified Kashmir through Baltistan conquest. Three sons from two Hindu queens (daughters of Raja of Jammu).
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Hindola Mahal (Mandu)
nodes.detail: 'Swing Palace' at Mandu, built c.1425 under Hushang Shah. Named for sloping outer walls that give the illusion of a swinging building. T-shaped hall; massive buttressed walls with fine stone screens. Used as durbar hall. Exemplifies the Malwa School's use of batter.

nodes.label: Rana Kumbha
nodes.detail: Mewar ruler (1433-68) who made it the premier Rajput state. Defeated internal rivals; conquered Bundi, Kotah, Dungarpur. Fought Malwa and Gujarat simultaneously; repulsed multiple Kumbhalgarh sieges by Gujarat. Built Kirti Stambha (Tower of Victory) at Chittor — 9-storey tower commemorating victory over Mahmud Khalji of Malwa. Also built 32 forts including Kumbhalgarh. Learned author; patron of arts. Murdered by his son Uda for the throne.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Mahmud Khalji of Malwa
nodes.detail: Most powerful Malwa sultan (1436-69). Restless and ambitious — fought Gujarat, Gondwana, Orissa, Bahmanis, and Delhi. Principal struggle against Rana Kumbha of Mewar. Destroyed temples during these campaigns — a lapse from Malwa's earlier tolerance, though not a general policy of temple destruction.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Kirti Stambha (Chittor)
nodes.detail: 9-storey Tower of Victory built by Rana Kumbha at Chittor (c.1448) to commemorate his victory over Mahmud Khalji of Malwa. Covered in sculptures of Hindu deities. Contrast with the older Jain Kirti Stambha at the same site (Chittor has two famous Jain and Hindu victory towers). Architectural statement of Rajput resurgence.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Ashrafi Mahal (Mandu)
nodes.detail: 'Palace of Gold Coins' at Mandu, built by Mahmud Khalji next to the Jami Masjid — originally a madarasa, expanded into a victory tower commemorating his defeat of Rana Kumbha. The Seven-Storey Tower (mostly ruined) intended to parallel the Kirti Stambha of Chittor. Mostly in ruins today.

nodes.label: Mahmud Begarha
nodes.detail: Most famous Gujarat sultan (1459-1511). Name 'Begarha' from capturing two major garhs — Girnar/Junagadh (1469) and Champaner (1484). Founded Mustafabad below Girnar and Muhammadabad near Champaner. Sacked Dwarka (cited pirate harbouring, also razed temples). Allied with Egypt against Portuguese naval threat. Striking appearance — beard to waist, moustache tied over head. Barbosa: nourished on poison from childhood (insects died on contact). Legendary appetite (10-15 kg/day). Made Gujarat powerful enough to later challenge Humayun.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Jahaz Mahal (Mandu)
nodes.detail: 'Ship Palace' at Mandu, built by Ghiyas-ud-din Khalji (1469-1500). Long two-storey building (120m × 15m) between two artificial lakes (Munj Talao, Kapur Talao), appearing to float like a ship. Terraces, pavilions and cupolas on top. Showpiece of Malwa School's use of water and environmental adaptation.

nodes.label: Alauddin Hussain Shah
nodes.detail: Bengal sultan (1493-1519), presided over its brilliant cultural phase. Inducted Hindus in highest offices — wazir, physician, chief of bodyguard, mint-master were all Hindus. Rupa and Sanatana Goswami (Chaitanya's chief lieutenants) held senior posts before renouncing. Showed great respect to Chaitanya. Patronised Bengali literature — his son Nusrat Shah had Mahabharata translated to Bengali. Conquered Kamata (Cooch Bihar), wrested Chittagong from Arakan, annexed Tipperah.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Nimatnama
nodes.detail: 'Book of Delicacies' — illustrated cookery and pharmacy manuscript produced at Mandu during the reign of Nasir Shah Khalji (1500-10) and completed under Mahmud Shah II. Famous example of Sultanate miniature painting — synthesis of Persian Shiraz-school style with indigenous Indian elements. Depicts sultan supervising preparation of dishes and recipes for foods/remedies. Preserved in the British Library.

nodes.label: Rani Roopmati Pavilion (Mandu)
nodes.detail: Hilltop pavilion at Mandu, originally a military observation post later associated with Rani Roopmati (wife of Baz Bahadur, last Malwa sultan, defeated by Akbar 1561). Affords views of the Narmada — Roopmati reportedly refused to eat until she had seen the river.

nodes.label: Rana Sanga (Sangram Singh)
nodes.detail: Mewar ruler (1508-28), grandson of Rana Kumbha. Defeated Malwa's Mahmud II at Khatoli 1517, carried him prisoner to Chittor, annexed eastern Malwa including Chanderi. Defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Khatoli and Dholpur. Invited Babur to oust the Lodis, hoping to emerge as dominant north Indian power. Defeated by Babur at Khanwa 1527 (Babur's victory consolidated Mughal rule).
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Qadam Rasul Mosque (Gaur)
nodes.detail: Single-domed mosque at Gaur (West Bengal) built 1530 by Nusrat Shah (son of Alauddin Hussain Shah). Houses an impression of the Prophet's footprint (qadam rasul) brought from Mecca. Late Bengal Sultanate style — brick construction with curved Bangla roof, stone veneer, blind arches.

nodes.label: Malik Muhammad Jaisi
nodes.detail: Hindi/Awadhi Sufi poet of the Jaunpur tradition. Composed Padmavat (c.1540) — an allegorical Sufi masnavi set around Alauddin Khalji's siege of Chittor (1303), introducing the Padmini legend more than two centuries after the event. Representative of Sufi saints composing in Hindi to convey mystical concepts to common people.

nodes.label: Sayyid Dynasty
nodes.detail: Delhi dynasty (1414-51) that arose after Timur's 1398 invasion. Nominal rule — contemporaries quipped the sultan's writ ran 'from Delhi to Palam'. Khizr Khan (founder, claimed Sayyid descent from Prophet) and successors ruled a rump territory while regional governors broke away. Displaced by Bahlul Lodi who crowned himself in 1451 after the Sayyid king Alam Shah died in exile.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Bahlul Lodi
nodes.detail: Founder of the Lodi dynasty (1451-89). Afghan noble of Sirhind who dominated Punjab after checking the Khokhars. Occupied Delhi 1451 when Sayyid king died in exile. Fought the Sharqis of Jaunpur across several decades; invited Afghans of Roh to India, changing the complexion of Muslim society. Annexed Jaunpur 1484. Divided kingdom among sons and relations — a partition later undone by Sikandar.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Lodi Dynasty
nodes.detail: Afghan dynasty (1451-1526) founded by Bahlul Lodi; first non-Turkish dynasty of Delhi. Bahlul (1451-89), Sikandar Lodi (1489-1517), Ibrahim Lodi (1517-26). Expanded the Afghan element in north Indian Muslim society — many Afghans of Roh migrated on Bahlul's invitation. Annexed Sharqi kingdom of Jaunpur 1484. Ended at First Battle of Panipat 1526 (Babur).
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Sikandar Lodi
nodes.detail: Lodi sultan (1489-1517). Controlled Afghan nobles by requiring them to stand in durbar and show deference — a departure from their tradition of first-among-equals. Laid foundation of Agra (1506) to control eastern Rajasthan/Malwa/Gujarat routes. Introduced gazz-i-Sikandari (standard yard) which prevailed till Mughal times. Abolished octroi on grains. Bigoted in later reign — re-imposed jizyah, demolished temples (Nagarkot), executed a Brahman for teaching Hindu-Muslim scriptural equivalence. Patron of Persian scholars; many Sanskrit works (including music treatises) translated to Persian under him.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Double Dome (Lodi Innovation)
nodes.detail: Architectural innovation of the Lodi period — a hollow inner dome beneath the outer dome. Reasons: (1) greater structural strength; (2) lowering inner ceiling for human scale while retaining commanding outer skyline. First full expression in Sikander Lodi's tomb at Lodi Garden. Adopted and refined by Mughals — Humayun's Tomb is the first major Mughal double dome, culminating in the Taj Mahal. Lodi tombs also feature hard/bare exteriors (octagonal, ~15m diameter) on sloping verandahs.

nodes.label: Lodi Tomb Architecture
nodes.detail: Lodi-era style (c.1451-1526): tombs placed on high platforms for better skyline; many octagonal (~15m diameter) on sloping verandahs. Signature innovation — the double dome (hollow inner dome beneath outer dome, giving strength + lowering inner ceiling). Hard, bare, less decorated exteriors. Some tombs set in gardens. Lodi Garden (Delhi) preserves Muhammad Shah's tomb, Sikandar Lodi's tomb, Bara Gumbad, Sheesh Gumbad. Features (double domes, octagonal plans, garden-tombs) adopted by Mughals — culminating in Humayun's tomb and the Taj Mahal.

nodes.label: Lodi Khuladar
nodes.detail: Sultanate miniature painting style prevalent in the region between Delhi and Jaunpur during late 15th-early 16th c. Blended Persian illumination with indigenous Indian elements; formed the 'Sultanate formulae' that the later Mughal, Rajput, and Deccan schools all drew from. Less refined than the Nimatnama school of Mandu but historically important as precursor of Mughal painting.

nodes.label: Agra (founded 1506)
nodes.detail: Founded by Sikandar Lodi in 1506 after careful site survey. Intended to command eastern Rajasthan, Malwa, and routes to Gujarat. Became the second capital of the Lodis. Later chosen by the Mughals (Babur, Akbar, Shah Jahan) as imperial capital — site of the Taj Mahal and Agra Fort.
nodes.chapter_title: Struggle for Empire North India I (1400-1525)

nodes.label: Sher Shah Sur
nodes.detail: Afghan leader who defeated Humayun and drove him into exile (1540-45). Established efficient administration and revenue system during his brief rule. His administrative innovations influenced later Mughal governance. Built Grand Trunk Road from Peshawar to Bengal.
nodes.chapter_title: Kings and Chronicles - The Mughal Courts

nodes.label: Bhils
nodes.detail: Large tribe spread across western and central India. By late 16th century many became settled agriculturists and some zamindars, though many clans remained hunter-gatherers. Adapted to changing conditions.

nodes.label: Mundas and Santals
nodes.detail: Important tribal groups in present-day Bihar, Jharkhand, Orissa and Bengal. Along with Cheros, they represented significant tribal presence in eastern India that interacted with Mughal power.

nodes.label: Rajput Clans
nodes.detail: New Rajput clans became powerful by 11th-12th centuries from lineages including Hunas, Chandelas and Chalukyas. Some had been tribes earlier. Replaced older rulers in agricultural areas and set example for tribal peoples.

nodes.label: Medieval Tribal Societies
nodes.detail: Many subcontinent societies did not follow Brahmanical rules or divide into unequal classes. United by kinship bonds. Obtained livelihood from agriculture, hunting-gathering or herding. Controlled land jointly.

nodes.label: Nomadic Pastoralists
nodes.detail: Mobile people who moved long distances with animals, living on milk and pastoral products. Exchanged wool, ghee with settled agriculturists. Included Gaddis in the western Himalaya.

nodes.label: Gond Kingdom
nodes.detail: Gonds lived in Gondwana practising shifting cultivation. Garha Katanga had 70,000 villages. Kingdom divided into garhs, chaurasi (84 villages) and barhots (12 villages). Rani Durgawati resisted Mughal forces in 1565.

nodes.label: Garha Katanga
nodes.detail: Rich Gond state that earned wealth by trapping and exporting wild elephants. When Mughals defeated the Gonds, they captured precious coins and elephants. Part annexed, rest granted to Chandra Shah.

nodes.label: Rani Durgawati
nodes.detail: Capable ruler of Gond kingdom Garha Katanga, ruling on behalf of her young son Bir Narain. Expanded the kingdom considerably. Defeated by Mughal forces under Asaf Khan in 1565. Preferred death to surrender.

nodes.label: Ahom Kingdom
nodes.detail: Mongoloid tribe from north Burma who established kingdom in Brahmaputra valley 1228. Gradually Hinduised — Suhungmung (1497-1539), considered greatest Ahom ruler, took name Svarga Narayana; his reign saw rapid Sanskritisation and Vaishnava reform (Shankaradeva). Used firearms from 1530s; made gunpowder by 1660s. Repulsed Bengal Sultanate attack (probably Nusrat Shah). Used paiks (forced labour) with census-based rotation and buranjis (historical works in Ahom then Assamese). Defeated Mughals at Battle of Saraighat 1671 (Lachit Borphukan). Kingdom lasted until Burmese invasion / British annexation 1826.

nodes.label: Banjaras
nodes.detail: Most important trader-nomads. Caravans called tanda with up to 700 persons and 14,000 oxen. Carried grain for Alauddin Khalji and Mughal armies. Bought grain cheaply and sold where dearer.

nodes.label: Buranjis
nodes.detail: Historical works written by the Ahoms, first in Ahom language then in Assamese. Represent sophisticated literary culture. Important works of Sanskrit were also translated into local language.

nodes.label: Paiks (Ahom Forced Labour)
nodes.detail: People forced to work for the Ahom state. Census taken to determine numbers. Villages sent paiks by rotation. Adults served in army during war, otherwise built dams, irrigation and public works.

nodes.label: Shifting Cultivation
nodes.detail: Method where trees and bushes are cut and burnt, crops sown in ashes. When soil loses fertility, another plot is cleared. Practised by Gonds and other forest-dwelling tribal communities.

nodes.label: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq
nodes.detail: Founder of Tughlaq dynasty (1320-25). Rose as officer by defeating Khusrau Khan. Died 1325 when a wooden pavilion hastily erected by his son Muhammad Tughlaq collapsed during an elephant parade — rumours of parricide followed. Built the massive palace-fortress complex Tughlaqabad near Delhi, with an artificial lake formed by blocking the Yamuna. His tomb introduced the marble-dome-on-high-platform style in Sultanate architecture.

nodes.label: Tughlaqabad
nodes.detail: Massive palace-fortress complex built by Ghiyasuddin and Muhammad Tughlaq near Delhi. Huge artificial lake created by blocking the Yamuna. Sloping walls (batter) gave an effect of strength and solidity — a Tughlaq hallmark. Ghiyasuddin's tomb within the complex — on a high platform with a marble dome, marking a new architectural trend. Abandoned after Muhammad Tughlaq shifted court to Daulatabad.

nodes.label: Muhammad bin Tughlaq
nodes.detail: Tughlaq sultan (1324-51), son of Ghiyasuddin. Called 'ill-starred idealist' — deeply read in philosophy and science, conversed with Muslim mystics, Hindu yogis, and Jain saints (Jinaprabha Suri); accused of 'rationalism' by theologians. Gave offices on merit, not lineage. Five major experiments: (1) transfer of capital to Daulatabad 1327 (~1500 km forced exodus); (2) bronze token currency 1329-30 (failed due to forgery); (3) increased doab taxation leading to peasant rebellion and famine; (4) diwan-i-amir-i-kohi development-bloc agricultural scheme; (5) Khurasan expedition army (disbanded) and Qarachil (Kumaon hills) expedition (disaster, 10 of 10,000 returned). Appointed Ibn Battuta qazi of Delhi. Died 1351 in Sind while suppressing rebellion. Vijayanagara (Harihara-Bukka) and Bahmani (Hasan Gangu) both emerged from rebellions against him.

nodes.label: Shift to Daulatabad
nodes.detail: Muhammad Tughlaq's 1327 order shifting Delhi residents — especially officers, Sufi saints, and leading men — to Deogir (renamed Daulatabad) to better control the south. Road built with rest-houses for the 1500 km journey; liberal grants made; but summer-season exodus caused many deaths and homesickness. Ordinary population not moved; Delhi remained populous, coins minted there confirm. After a few years the shift was abandoned — couldn't control north from south either. Long-range consequences: brought north-south closer; religious and cultural ideas (Sufi saints) spread into Deccan; basis for Deccan Islamic culture (including the later Bahmani).

nodes.label: Muhammad Tughluq's Token Currency
nodes.detail: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's bronze/brass coin (1329-30) intended to have the same value as the silver tanka — following the successful precedent of Qublai Khan of China and Ghazan Khan of Iran. Introduced due to shortage of silver in 14th-century world. The government failed to prevent forgery; devaluation in markets. Withdrawn; sultan promised to exchange silver for bronze — many did so, but forged coins (detectable by tests) weren't exchanged and 'lay heaped up outside the fort for many years' (Barani). Damaged prestige and treasury but the government recovered; Ibn Battuta in 1333 found no lasting harm.

nodes.label: Firuz Shah Tughlaq
nodes.detail: Tughlaq sultan (1351-88), cousin of Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Appeased nobles by making iqtas hereditary; extended heredity to army. Dug extensive canals (longest Sutlej-Hansi, 200 km; Yamuna canal). Built new towns — Hissar-Firuzah, Firuzabad, Fatehabad, Jaunpur. Established karkhanas with 1,80,000 slaves. Made jizyah a separate tax; imposed it on Brahmans. Had Sanskrit works (music, medicine, Rajatarangini) translated to Persian. Set up free hospitals, banned mutilation punishments, provided dowries to poor girls. Orthodox on religion — persecuted Muslim sects deemed heretical; burnt a Brahman for preaching to Muslims.

nodes.label: Hauz Khas
nodes.detail: Firuz Shah Tughlaq's pleasure resort around a large tank originally built by Alauddin Khalji. Contains a madarasa, pavilions, and Firuz's own tomb. Characteristic Tughlaq combination of arch-and-dome with lintel-and-beam. Used greystone (cheaper than red sandstone); minimal decoration apart from lotus motif. Now a South Delhi park.

nodes.label: Timur (Tamerlane)
nodes.detail: Central Asian conqueror (1336-1405); Turk claiming blood relationship with Changez Khan. Unified Iran and Turan, extending empire from Volga to Indus and Syria to southern Russia. 1398 invasion of Delhi — plundering raid. Mercilessly sacked towns along the way; sacked Delhi without mercy, large numbers of Hindus and Muslims killed; took enormous wealth and many Indian artisans (masons, stone-cutters, carpenters) to Samarqand. Direct political effect on India small — but marked the end of strong Delhi Sultanate rule and triggered the rise of regional sultanates (Malwa, Gujarat, Jaunpur, Bengal) and the Sayyid/Lodi rumps.

nodes.label: Caste System (Traveller Accounts)
nodes.detail: Al-Biruni described the four varnas based on Sanskrit texts, finding parallels in Persian social categories. Disapproved of pollution concept as contrary to nature. Ibn Battuta and Bernier also commented on social stratification. Antyaja ('born outside system') provided labour.

nodes.label: Ibn Battuta
nodes.detail: Moroccan traveller born in Tangier, arrived in India 1333. Appointed qazi of Delhi by Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Travelled extensively across North Africa, West Asia, Central Asia, India, China. His Rihla records detailed observations of 14th-century Indian social life.

nodes.label: Sultanate Postal System (Dak Chauki)
nodes.detail: (Described by Ibn Battuta during Tughlaq-era Delhi Sultanate, not Mughal. Relabelled for accuracy.) Ibn Battuta described an efficient postal system with horse relay (uluq) and foot relay stations at regular intervals. Enabled rapid communication across the empire. Foot carriers were considered even more reliable than horse system for important messages.

nodes.label: Persian Historical Texts (Tawarikh)
nodes.detail: Persian historical writing developed strongly in Sultanate India. Major historians — Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani (Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, covering till Balban), Ziauddin Barani (Tarikh-i-Firuzshahi, Fatawa-i-Jahandari — covering Balban to early Firuz; key source for market controls and politics), Shams-i-Siraj Afif (second Tarikh-i-Firuzshahi, focused on Firuz), Isami (Futuh-us-Salatin, mid-14c, Bahmani court). Amir Khusrau's historical mathnavis (Qiranus-Sadain, Miftahul Futuh, Khazainul Futuh, Tughlaq Nama) blur poetry and history. Later — Yahya Sirhindi (Tarikh-i-Mubarakshahi, Sayyid period), Ferishta (17c but covers Sultanate).

nodes.label: Rihla
nodes.detail: Ibn Battuta's travel account written in Arabic, dictated after his return to Morocco. Records unfamiliar customs, foods (coconut, paan), the postal system (horse and foot relay), and dangers of travel. Journey from Multan to Delhi took 40 days, Sind to Delhi 50 days.

nodes.label: Ziyauddin Barani
nodes.detail: 14th-century chronicler who wrote his chronicle first in 1356 and a revised version in 1358. The first version remained lost until the 1960s. Important source for Delhi Sultanate history.
